newsitem.title: UK: Blair to let commission rule on N.Irish parades.
newsitem.headline: Blair to let commission rule on N.Irish parades.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government said on Wednesday it would set up an independent commission to rule on controversial parades in Northern Ireland that have proved in the past to be flashpoints for sectarian violence.

The government said it would introduce a bill to implement in full the recommendations made in January by Peter North, a leading academic at Britain's Oxford University, aimed at reducing tension over parades in the British-ruled province.

Protestants, who are in a majority in Northern Ireland, hold a string of parades each year starting in late spring to demonstrate their loyalty to their faith and to the British crown. But the Catholic minority regards them as triumphalist commemorations of 300-year-old victories over the native Irish.

The main recommendation of North's report, which the government described as careful and even-handed, was to transfer responsibility for making decisions on contested marches from the police to a strengthened Parades Commission.
The commission's current role is limited to mediation and education.
The bill will allow the commission to take into account the wider effects of parades on community relations in Northern Ireland instead of concentrating solely on the implications for public order.

The previous Conservative government, buried in Labour's landslide victory in the May 1 election, commissioned North's report after a frenzy of sectarian violence last year touched off when Protestants insisted on marching through a Catholic area of Drumcree, a town 30 miles (48 km) south of Belfast.
The violence set back efforts to bring peace to the province after more than 25 years of strife.
Former prime minister John Major's government, faced with Protestant opposition to the North recommendations, delayed implementing them pending further consultation.

Blair's government, in a formal speech read by head of state Queen Elizabeth setting out its initial legislative programme, said it was determined to seek conciliation between the two communities and a political settlement commanding broad support.

Government officials declined to comment on newspaper reports that said Blair would underscore his commitment to peace in Northern Ireland by paying his first visit to the province as prime minister within days.
Multi-party talks on the political future of Northern Ireland are due to resume in Belfast on June 3.
The parades bill would provide a code of conduct regulating the conduct of marchers and protesters and create a new offence of incitement if the commission's rulings are flouted.
The commission would come to its decisions following consultation with the largely Protestant police force, the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC).
Under the proposed legislation, the chief constable of the RUC would have the right to refer the commission's decisions to Northern Irish Secretary Mo Mowlam.
The RUC would also retain a power to impose conditions on a parade if risks to public order made it impossible to enforce a commission ruling.
